transcript.content: Hi, welcome in — I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. [Name], it's... it's a lot of things, really, but I guess the main thing that finally made me make the appointment is my eating. It’s just gotten completely off track lately. I mean, some days I wake up and the thought of food is just... I don't know, it's almost exhausting. I’ll barely get down a cup of coffee and maybe a granola bar before I head in for a shift. And working in healthcare support, you know, you're on your feet, you're moving patients, you're running around, so you need the energy. But I just can't seem to force myself to eat a real meal. And I’ve really started to notice it, too. Like, my scrubs, the ones I've worn for a couple of years now, they’re just hanging loose on me. I have to pull the drawstrings so tight just to keep the pants up. And it's not like I'm trying to lose weight or go on a diet or anything like that. I just... I don't have the appetite, and the weight is just falling off me without me even trying. It's been going on for a while now, and I just keep thinking it'll get better, that I'll wake up hungry one day, but it hasn't happened.
Over the past few weeks, have you noticed a change in your mood, like feeling sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah... yeah, I have. I don't even know if "sad" is the right word for it, really. It's more like... well, you know how I mentioned my mornings before, with the coffee and everything? I've been trying to figure out how to explain it to myself. Most mornings, my alarm goes off at 4:45 AM, because I usually like to have a little time to myself before the shift starts, just to ease into things. But lately, I wake up and I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling. 

I wake up with this... this incredibly heavy, almost hollow feeling right in the center of my chest. It's like the entire day is already completely ruined before I even get out from under the covers, you know? Before I even put on my hospital badge. I'll just look over at my lanyard sitting on the nightstand, and the thought of clipping it on and walking through those doors just feels impossible. 

I used to actually enjoy my morning routine—I'd watch the local news, check the weather, maybe read a bit on my phone. But now, all of that just feels so pointless. I have zero interest in the news or anything else I used to like. I just feel this dragging, empty weight, and it takes every single ounce of willpower I have just to put my feet on the floor. It's just this dark, hollow cloud that sits on me from the second I open my eyes, and I just keep wondering how I'm supposed to get through another twelve-hour shift feeling this way.
Besides the appetite and mood changes, have you noticed any unexplained fevers, night sweats, or new lumps or swelling anywhere, like in your neck, armpits, or groin?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I check my temperature sometimes at work, you know, just out of habit because we have the thermometers right there at the nurses' station, the temporal ones that just scan across the forehead. And it's always normal, always right around 98.6 or maybe 97.9, depending on the time of day. I haven't had any fevers at all. And night sweats... well, sometimes I wake up feeling a little warm, but I think that's just because I sleep with a heavy comforter. I've always liked the weight of it, it helps me feel grounded, I guess. But I'm not waking up drenched or anything where I have to change my sheets. It's not like that. And as for lumps or swelling, no, I haven't noticed anything like that either. I mean, I shower every day, obviously, and I feel like I'd notice if there was something new or weird going on in my neck or under my arms. You hear stories, working in the hospital, you see patients come in with these swollen lymph nodes and it turns out to be something awful, so I'm pretty hyper-aware of my own body in that regard. But no, nothing like that. It's just... it's just the weight loss and this heavy feeling I was talking about. I keep checking my neck when I shave, just to be sure, but it's all completely normal.
When you notice your clothes fitting looser, how do you feel about that weight loss—are you happy or relieved about it, or does it worry you?

Happy? Oh, no, definitely not happy. Honestly, it's... it's actually really unsettling. Like I was saying before, I'm not on a diet or anything. I know a lot of the folks I work with, especially some of the nurses on the floor, they're always talking about intermittent fasting or doing keto or whatever the new trend is, and they get so thrilled when they drop a few pounds. But for me, it just feels wrong. It really worries me, actually. 

I put on my jeans the other day—just my regular everyday Levi's that I always wear on my days off when I'm just running to the grocery store or the pharmacy—and I had to notch my belt two whole holes tighter. Two holes! And even then, the denim just looked all baggy and... I don't know, just sad on me. It really freaked me out for a minute. It worries me because it feels like my body is just shrinking, and I'm not doing anything to cause it on purpose, other than just not being able to stomach the thought of eating. It feels like my body is kind of failing me, or maybe I'm failing it, but I just don't have the energy to fix it. 

So yeah, I'm definitely not relieved. If anything, it just adds to that whole heavy, dragging feeling I told you about, because now I'm lying there in bed staring at the ceiling, thinking about how my clothes don't fit and how I'm just sort of wasting away, and I still can't bring myself to even make a piece of toast. It's just this constant, physical reminder every time I get dressed that something is really off track with me.
Have you noticed any tremors in your hands, a racing or pounding heartbeat, or feeling unusually hot or intolerant of warm environments recently?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, my hands are pretty steady. They have to be, you know, for my job. When I'm helping transfer a patient from the bed to the chair, or adjusting their IV lines—not that I start the IVs, but I help make sure the tubing isn't tangled when we move them—I need to have a good grip. If my hands were shaking, I think I'd notice, and the nurses would definitely notice. Sometimes I'll hold my hand out in front of me just to check, just because I get anxious about things, but it's always steady. 

And my heart... no, it doesn't really race or pound. If anything, it feels like everything in me is just moving in slow motion these days. Like I said about that heavy feeling in the mornings, it's almost like my heart is just barely thudding along, just doing the absolute bare minimum to keep me going. I don't get those sudden bursts where it feels like it's beating out of my chest. I know what that feels like—I had a panic attack once, years ago, back when I was still in school for my associate's degree, right before finals. My heart was going a mile a minute then, but I haven't had anything like that recently.

As for feeling hot... well, I mentioned the heavy comforter earlier, right? I'm usually the one who's a little chilly, if anything. The hospital is always kept freezing cold, especially on the surgical floors, so I'm used to wearing my long-sleeve undershirts beneath my scrubs. Even when I'm running around, doing a million things, answering call bells, I don't really break a sweat or feel overheated. I definitely don't feel intolerant to the heat. Honestly, a warm room sounds kind of nice right now, compared to how cold and empty everything else feels. So, no, no tremors, no racing heart, and definitely not feeling too hot. Just... just the same slow, heavy drag.
Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or wishing you weren't alive?

Hurting myself? No, no, I haven't made any kind of plan to do anything like that. I mean, working at the hospital, sometimes I get pulled from my regular duties to act as a 1:1 sitter for patients who are on suicide watch. I sit in the room with them for my whole twelve-hour shift, just watching them, making sure they're safe. I see what that kind of thing does to them, and I see the families when they come to visit, so I know the reality of it. Because of that, no, I haven't sat down and tried to figure out a way to actually hurt myself. 

But... the other part of your question, about wishing I wasn't alive... yeah. I do. I catch myself thinking that a lot lately, actually. It's usually at night when I'm lying in bed, like I was telling you before, under that heavy comforter. I'll just be lying there, staring up at the dark ceiling, maybe listening to the hum of the refrigerator in the kitchen or a car driving by outside, and I just start wishing that I just wouldn't wake up. 

It just seems like it would be so much easier if I just... disappeared. Just faded away in my sleep. Because the thought of that alarm going off at 5:00 AM, and having to force myself to get up, and drag this heavy, tired body into the shower, put on my scrubs, and go pretend to be okay for a whole shift... it just feels like entirely too much. It's not that I want to do something violent to make it happen, I just... I get so tired of feeling like this dragging, empty shell, and I think, wouldn't it be a relief if I just wasn't here tomorrow? If the world just kept turning and I was just gone? It's a really unsettling thing to catch yourself thinking, but it just sneaks up on me when the apartment is quiet and I'm alone with my thoughts.
How long has this heavy, hollow feeling and loss of interest been going on—would you say it's been more than two weeks now?

Two weeks? Oh, gosh, no. I wish it had only been two weeks. If it had only been two weeks, I think I could probably just brush it off as a bad patch, you know? Like maybe I just caught a bug going around the hospital, or I was just stressed about some new protocol they rolled out on the floor. But no, it's been way, way longer than that. 

I actually remember pretty clearly when this specific feeling—this heavy, hollow, dragging feeling where I just don't care about anything anymore—really settled in. It was... well, it's been roughly a year and four months now. I know that sounds really specific, but I remember it because it was right around the time they switched the parking assignments for the staff at the hospital. They made all the support staff park in the satellite lot, the one that's a good four blocks away, and we had to start taking this little shuttle bus in. 

I remember sitting on that shuttle bus one morning, looking out the window at the rain—it was a Tuesday, I think, and it was pouring—and just feeling this absolute, crushing weight drop onto me. It wasn't just being tired from the walk or annoyed about the parking. It was this deep, settling realization that I just didn't want to do any of it anymore. And it wasn't a passing thought. It just stayed. 

Before that, things were... different. I mean, I had other things going on, other struggles that I'm sure we'll get into, but this steady, constant depression? This feeling like my battery is completely drained and won't recharge no matter how long I lie under that comforter? That really locked in about a year and four months ago. 

Since then, it's just been every single day. Every morning on that shuttle bus, every time I clock in, every time I go to the grocery store and just stare at the shelves because nothing sounds good. It's like someone turned down the volume and the color on my whole life, and they just left it that way for over a year. So yeah, definitely more than two weeks. It feels like it's been a lifetime, honestly, but if I look at the calendar, it's been about sixteen months of just... this.

Have you experienced anything like hearing voices, seeing things that others don't see, or having unusual beliefs—like feeling you're being punished or that something terrible is happening to your body—during this time?

Voices... yeah. Yeah, I do hear things. And the other stuff you mentioned, about unusual beliefs... it's really hard to talk about, because I know how it sounds, especially working in healthcare, but... it's just so real to me. 

See, at the hospital, we have to chart everything. Every single thing. Every time I take a set of vitals, every time I empty a Foley catheter, every time I help turn a patient every two hours so they don't get bedsores, I have to log into one of those computers on wheels—we call them COWs—and put it all into the system. But lately, I get this overwhelming feeling, this absolute certainty, that people are tracking my charting. Like they are watching every single keystroke I make, analyzing the timestamps, just waiting and watching me through the system. I don't even know exactly who is doing it, if it's administration or someone else entirely, but I can feel them tracking me. 

And then there are the voices. It's like this whispering, or sometimes it's louder, just right there in my ear when I'm standing in the hallway or even when I'm right in the middle of a patient's room. They say things about me, commenting on what I'm doing, telling me I'm messing up. 

And you'd think—at least, I would think—that with how completely drained I am from that heavy, awful depression I was just telling you about, maybe my brain would just be too tired to do all the other stuff. But it's not. That's the worst part of it all. When the depression is at its absolute worst, when I feel like I'm moving through wet cement and I'm just wishing I could disappear... the voices and the feeling that people are tracking my charting are still right there with it. 

So I’m fighting both at the same time during shifts. I'm dragging this hollow, exhausted body down the fluorescent hallways, trying not to just collapse, and at the exact same time, I'm hearing these voices, and I'm absolutely terrified to type a patient's blood pressure into the computer because I know I'm being monitored. It's just exhausting. I mean, the physical work is hard enough, lifting people and being on your feet for twelve hours, but the mental gymnastics of trying to act completely normal while you're fighting this two-front war in your own head... it just takes everything out of you. Sometimes I'll just go into the clean supply closet and stand there staring at the stacks of extra blankets, just trying to catch my breath, because fighting the heavy feeling and the voices and the tracking all at once... it's just too much.
Have there been times when you were not feeling that heavy, depressed mood at all, but you still heard the voices or felt that people were tracking your charting?

Yeah... yeah, actually, there was a time like that. It’s funny you ask, because I remember thinking it was so strange. There was this period when that heavy, wet cement feeling I was telling you about actually eased up. It lifted enough that I felt almost like my old self. I even started running a little again. I used to jog around my neighborhood, just a couple of miles to clear my head, and I had completely stopped doing that when the hollow feeling set in. But for a little bit there, I was actually lacing up my sneakers, getting outside, and just getting through the day without feeling like I was dragging a thousand pounds behind me. I’d wake up and the alarm wouldn’t feel like a punishment. 

But the weird thing is, the other stuff didn't stop. You'd think if my mood was better, my head would clear out entirely, right? But it didn't. For several weeks, even while I was feeling physically okay and getting through my shifts just fine, I was still dealing with it. I’d be walking down to the basement level to grab a bariatric wheelchair or something—totally empty hallway, nobody around at all, just me and the hum of the fluorescent lights—and I’d still hear those comments. Just whispering right there, criticizing me. 

And it wasn't just the voices, either. We have this big printed schedule they pin up on the corkboard in the breakroom, right by the time clock. Even when I was feeling good and running and eating normally, I kept reading that schedule over and over like it had hidden warnings about me. I'd look at the grid and think, okay, why did they shift my lunch break by fifteen minutes? Why am I suddenly floating to the fourth floor on Thursday? I was absolutely convinced whoever was making the schedule was using it to send me coded messages, warning me that they were watching me or that I was in trouble. I’d stand there with my coffee, feeling totally fine energy-wise, but just obsessing over the highlighters and the shift assignments, trying to decode it. So, yeah, even when the depression took a break, that other stuff... it was still right there with me for weeks.
That period when your mood improved and you were running again but still hearing the voices and feeling tracked—about how many weeks did that stretch last?

Well, let me think about that... how many weeks exactly. It’s hard to say precisely, because when you work in healthcare, time just sort of blurs together, you know? You’ve got your three twelves, or sometimes you pick up an extra shift because they’re short-staffed and they offer double time, and suddenly a week is gone and you don’t even know what day it is. But... if I really sit down and think about it, looking back at that specific time when I was lacing up my sneakers again and getting out there... 

I’d say it was a solid three, maybe four weeks. Yeah, about a month, give or take a few days. I remember because I had just bought a new pair of running shoes—these bright blue Asics, they have great arch support, which you really need when you're on your feet as much as I am—and I was breaking them in. And during that whole time, that whole three or four-week stretch, my mood was actually okay. Like I said, the heavy, dragging feeling was gone. I wasn't dreading the alarm clock. I was getting up, going for my run, making my coffee, and going into work feeling physically fine. 

But, like I was telling you, the other stuff just wouldn't quit. For that entire month, I’d be walking down to the basement level, completely alone in those empty hallways with just the hum of the fluorescent lights, and I’d still hear those voices making comments about me. Just whispering away. And the breakroom schedule... oh man, I spent that whole three or four weeks just staring at that corkboard. Every single day I clocked in, I’d stand there with my coffee, feeling totally fine energy-wise, but just obsessing over the highlighters and the shift assignments, absolutely convinced it was full of hidden warnings about me. So, yeah, I'd say it was a good three to four weeks where my mood had eased up, but I was still dealing with the voices and the schedule stuff every single day.

doctor.intent: Establish the primary reason for today's visit

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that my eating has gotten so off that some days I barely get down coffee and a granola bar before a shift, and my scrubs have been hanging loose even though I’m not trying to lose weight.
target_item.reason: This is the first turn of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S026.

patient.answer: Well, Dr. [Name], it's... it's a lot of things, really, but I guess the main thing that finally made me make the appointment is my eating. It’s just gotten completely off track lately. I mean, some days I wake up and the thought of food is just... I don't know, it's almost exhausting. I’ll barely get down a cup of coffee and maybe a granola bar before I head in for a shift. And working in healthcare support, you know, you're on your feet, you're moving patients, you're running around, so you need the energy. But I just can't seem to force myself to eat a real meal. And I’ve really started to notice it, too. Like, my scrubs, the ones I've worn for a couple of years now, they’re just hanging loose on me. I have to pull the drawstrings so tight just to keep the pants up. And it's not like I'm trying to lose weight or go on a diet or anything like that. I just... I don't have the appetite, and the weight is just falling off me without me even trying. It's been going on for a while now, and I just keep thinking it'll get better, that I'll wake up hungry one day, but it hasn't happened.

inference.note: Initial presentation of unintentional weight loss and appetite loss; differential includes depression, anxiety, hyperthyroidism, occult malignancy, malabsorption/GI disease, and eating disorder, pending further history on mood, medical symptoms, and psychological factors.

doctor.intent: Assess for depressive symptoms (mood, interest/pleasure) to differentiate major depressive disorder from other causes of appetite loss and weight loss
doctor.question: Over the past few weeks, have you noticed a change in your mood, like feeling sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling like the day is already ruined before I even put on my badge.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have been feeling sad, down, or have lost interest in things, which directly maps to depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah... yeah, I have. I don't even know if "sad" is the right word for it, really. It's more like... well, you know how I mentioned my mornings before, with the coffee and everything? I've been trying to figure out how to explain it to myself. Most mornings, my alarm goes off at 4:45 AM, because I usually like to have a little time to myself before the shift starts, just to ease into things. But lately, I wake up and I just lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling. 

I wake up with this... this incredibly heavy, almost hollow feeling right in the center of my chest. It's like the entire day is already completely ruined before I even get out from under the covers, you know? Before I even put on my hospital badge. I'll just look over at my lanyard sitting on the nightstand, and the thought of clipping it on and walking through those doors just feels impossible. 

I used to actually enjoy my morning routine—I'd watch the local news, check the weather, maybe read a bit on my phone. But now, all of that just feels so pointless. I have zero interest in the news or anything else I used to like. I just feel this dragging, empty weight, and it takes every single ounce of willpower I have just to put my feet on the floor. It's just this dark, hollow cloud that sits on me from the second I open my eyes, and I just keep wondering how I'm supposed to get through another twelve-hour shift feeling this way.

inference.note: The patient's report of early-morning awakening, pervasive anhedonia, and heavy/hollow mood strongly supports a major depressive episode (F32.9) as the primary driver of appetite loss and weight loss, reducing likelihood of an anxiety disorder (F41.1) since no anxious symptoms were described. Organic causes of weight loss (hyperthyroidism, malignancy, malabsorption) remain to be ruled out, and atypical eating disorder presentation is still possible though less likely given lack of body image concerns.

doctor.intent: Screen for systemic/constitutional symptoms (fevers, night sweats, swollen lymph nodes) that would suggest an underlying malignancy rather than a primary mood or eating disorder as the cause of weight loss
doctor.question: Besides the appetite and mood changes, have you noticed any unexplained fevers, night sweats, or new lumps or swelling anywhere, like in your neck, armpits, or groin?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical symptoms such as unexplained fevers, night sweats, or new lumps/swelling (lymphadenopathy) to rule out medical causes for weight loss, which are not covered in the psychiatric symptom profile.

patient.answer: No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I check my temperature sometimes at work, you know, just out of habit because we have the thermometers right there at the nurses' station, the temporal ones that just scan across the forehead. And it's always normal, always right around 98.6 or maybe 97.9, depending on the time of day. I haven't had any fevers at all. And night sweats... well, sometimes I wake up feeling a little warm, but I think that's just because I sleep with a heavy comforter. I've always liked the weight of it, it helps me feel grounded, I guess. But I'm not waking up drenched or anything where I have to change my sheets. It's not like that. And as for lumps or swelling, no, I haven't noticed anything like that either. I mean, I shower every day, obviously, and I feel like I'd notice if there was something new or weird going on in my neck or under my arms. You hear stories, working in the hospital, you see patients come in with these swollen lymph nodes and it turns out to be something awful, so I'm pretty hyper-aware of my own body in that regard. But no, nothing like that. It's just... it's just the weight loss and this heavy feeling I was talking about. I keep checking my neck when I shave, just to be sure, but it's all completely normal.

inference.note: Denial of fevers, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy lowers suspicion for malignancy (C80.1) but does not fully exclude it; absence of GI complaints keeps K90.9 low probability; strong depressive features (anhedonia, early morning awakening, hollow mood, unintentional appetite loss) reinforce F32.9 as leading diagnosis; F50.9 remains possible though patient denies intentional dieting, making it less likely; E05.9 still viable pending assessment of hyperthyroid symptoms like tremor or palpitations.

doctor.intent: Assess for body image distortion or fear of weight gain to differentiate an eating disorder from depression-related appetite loss
doctor.question: When you notice your clothes fitting looser, how do you feel about that weight loss—are you happy or relieved about it, or does it worry you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my attitude toward my weight loss to rule out an eating disorder (like anorexia nervosa). My symptom profile does not contain a specific item for body image or feelings about weight loss.

patient.answer:
Happy? Oh, no, definitely not happy. Honestly, it's... it's actually really unsettling. Like I was saying before, I'm not on a diet or anything. I know a lot of the folks I work with, especially some of the nurses on the floor, they're always talking about intermittent fasting or doing keto or whatever the new trend is, and they get so thrilled when they drop a few pounds. But for me, it just feels wrong. It really worries me, actually. 

I put on my jeans the other day—just my regular everyday Levi's that I always wear on my days off when I'm just running to the grocery store or the pharmacy—and I had to notch my belt two whole holes tighter. Two holes! And even then, the denim just looked all baggy and... I don't know, just sad on me. It really freaked me out for a minute. It worries me because it feels like my body is just shrinking, and I'm not doing anything to cause it on purpose, other than just not being able to stomach the thought of eating. It feels like my body is kind of failing me, or maybe I'm failing it, but I just don't have the energy to fix it. 

So yeah, I'm definitely not relieved. If anything, it just adds to that whole heavy, dragging feeling I told you about, because now I'm lying there in bed staring at the ceiling, thinking about how my clothes don't fit and how I'm just sort of wasting away, and I still can't bring myself to even make a piece of toast. It's just this constant, physical reminder every time I get dressed that something is really off track with me.

inference.note: Denial of fevers, night sweats, and lymphadenopathy reduces likelihood of malignancy (ruled out C80.1). Absence of GI symptoms argues against malabsorption (ruled out K90.9). Patient's distress about unintentional weight loss and lack of dieting behavior argues against an eating disorder (ruled out F50.9). Strong depressive symptoms (anhedonia, early morning heaviness, hopelessness, appetite loss) support F32.9; E05.9 remains possible as an organic cause of weight loss/appetite change pending further endocrine review.

doctor.intent: Assess for hyperthyroid symptoms such as heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, or racing heart to differentiate thyroid dysfunction from depression
doctor.question: Have you noticed any tremors in your hands, a racing or pounding heartbeat, or feeling unusually hot or intolerant of warm environments recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of hyperthyroidism (tremors, racing heartbeat, heat intolerance), which are not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, my hands are pretty steady. They have to be, you know, for my job. When I'm helping transfer a patient from the bed to the chair, or adjusting their IV lines—not that I start the IVs, but I help make sure the tubing isn't tangled when we move them—I need to have a good grip. If my hands were shaking, I think I'd notice, and the nurses would definitely notice. Sometimes I'll hold my hand out in front of me just to check, just because I get anxious about things, but it's always steady. 

And my heart... no, it doesn't really race or pound. If anything, it feels like everything in me is just moving in slow motion these days. Like I said about that heavy feeling in the mornings, it's almost like my heart is just barely thudding along, just doing the absolute bare minimum to keep me going. I don't get those sudden bursts where it feels like it's beating out of my chest. I know what that feels like—I had a panic attack once, years ago, back when I was still in school for my associate's degree, right before finals. My heart was going a mile a minute then, but I haven't had anything like that recently.

As for feeling hot... well, I mentioned the heavy comforter earlier, right? I'm usually the one who's a little chilly, if anything. The hospital is always kept freezing cold, especially on the surgical floors, so I'm used to wearing my long-sleeve undershirts beneath my scrubs. Even when I'm running around, doing a million things, answering call bells, I don't really break a sweat or feel overheated. I definitely don't feel intolerant to the heat. Honestly, a warm room sounds kind of nice right now, compared to how cold and empty everything else feels. So, no, no tremors, no racing heart, and definitely not feeling too hot. Just... just the same slow, heavy drag.

inference.note: Ruled out E05.9 (hyperthyroidism) given absence of tremor, tachycardia, heat intolerance, and reported cold intolerance; clinical picture remains consistent with major depressive episode with melancholic features (anorexia, weight loss, anhedonia, early morning awakening, psychomotor retardation).

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation given significant depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or wishing you weren't alive?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I haven’t made a plan to hurt myself, but I catch myself wishing I just wouldn’t wake up or thinking it would be easier if I disappeared.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, which matches the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
Hurting myself? No, no, I haven't made any kind of plan to do anything like that. I mean, working at the hospital, sometimes I get pulled from my regular duties to act as a 1:1 sitter for patients who are on suicide watch. I sit in the room with them for my whole twelve-hour shift, just watching them, making sure they're safe. I see what that kind of thing does to them, and I see the families when they come to visit, so I know the reality of it. Because of that, no, I haven't sat down and tried to figure out a way to actually hurt myself. 

But... the other part of your question, about wishing I wasn't alive... yeah. I do. I catch myself thinking that a lot lately, actually. It's usually at night when I'm lying in bed, like I was telling you before, under that heavy comforter. I'll just be lying there, staring up at the dark ceiling, maybe listening to the hum of the refrigerator in the kitchen or a car driving by outside, and I just start wishing that I just wouldn't wake up. 

It just seems like it would be so much easier if I just... disappeared. Just faded away in my sleep. Because the thought of that alarm going off at 5:00 AM, and having to force myself to get up, and drag this heavy, tired body into the shower, put on my scrubs, and go pretend to be okay for a whole shift... it just feels like entirely too much. It's not that I want to do something violent to make it happen, I just... I get so tired of feeling like this dragging, empty shell, and I think, wouldn't it be a relief if I just wasn't here tomorrow? If the world just kept turning and I was just gone? It's a really unsettling thing to catch yourself thinking, but it just sneaks up on me when the apartment is quiet and I'm alone with my thoughts.

inference.note: Denial of hyperthyroid symptoms (tremor, tachycardia, heat intolerance) reduces likelihood of thyrotoxicosis; no fever/night sweats/lymphadenopathy argues against infection or malignancy. Passive suicidal ideation without plan is consistent with severe MDE. No new features suggesting alternative diagnosis, so candidate list remains unchanged.

doctor.intent: Determine the duration of the depressive symptoms to confirm they meet the two-week minimum required for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: How long has this heavy, hollow feeling and loss of interest been going on—would you say it's been more than two weeks now?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: The steady depression and loss of interest settled in later, and it has been with me for roughly the past year and four months.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the depressive symptoms (heavy, hollow feeling and loss of interest), which corresponds to the depressive episode duration.

patient.answer:
Two weeks? Oh, gosh, no. I wish it had only been two weeks. If it had only been two weeks, I think I could probably just brush it off as a bad patch, you know? Like maybe I just caught a bug going around the hospital, or I was just stressed about some new protocol they rolled out on the floor. But no, it's been way, way longer than that. 

I actually remember pretty clearly when this specific feeling—this heavy, hollow, dragging feeling where I just don't care about anything anymore—really settled in. It was... well, it's been roughly a year and four months now. I know that sounds really specific, but I remember it because it was right around the time they switched the parking assignments for the staff at the hospital. They made all the support staff park in the satellite lot, the one that's a good four blocks away, and we had to start taking this little shuttle bus in. 

I remember sitting on that shuttle bus one morning, looking out the window at the rain—it was a Tuesday, I think, and it was pouring—and just feeling this absolute, crushing weight drop onto me. It wasn't just being tired from the walk or annoyed about the parking. It was this deep, settling realization that I just didn't want to do any of it anymore. And it wasn't a passing thought. It just stayed. 

Before that, things were... different. I mean, I had other things going on, other struggles that I'm sure we'll get into, but this steady, constant depression? This feeling like my battery is completely drained and won't recharge no matter how long I lie under that comforter? That really locked in about a year and four months ago. 

Since then, it's just been every single day. Every morning on that shuttle bus, every time I clock in, every time I go to the grocery store and just stare at the shelves because nothing sounds good. It's like someone turned down the volume and the color on my whole life, and they just left it that way for over a year. So yeah, definitely more than two weeks. It feels like it's been a lifetime, honestly, but if I look at the calendar, it's been about sixteen months of just... this.

inference.note: Symptom duration (~16 months), continuous heavy/hollow mood, anhedonia, unintentional weight loss, passive suicidal ideation, and psychomotor slowing support a severe major depressive episode (F32.2) rather than an unspecified one; ruled out hyperthyroid/infectious causes (no tremor, heat intolerance, fevers, lymphadenopathy) and anxiety/panic (no tachycardia or hyperarousal).

doctor.intent: Assess for psychotic features (hallucinations or delusions) to confirm severity without psychosis and support a specific severe depression diagnosis over an unspecified one
doctor.question: Have you experienced anything like hearing voices, seeing things that others don't see, or having unusual beliefs—like feeling you're being punished or that something terrible is happening to your body—during this time?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: When the depression is at its worst, the voices and the feeling that people are tracking my charting are still right there with it, so I’m fighting both at the same time during shifts.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I experienced psychotic symptoms like hearing voices or having unusual beliefs 'during this time' (referring to the period of depression discussed in the previous turn), which maps to the concurrent occurrence of psychotic symptoms and the depressive episode.

patient.answer:
Voices... yeah. Yeah, I do hear things. And the other stuff you mentioned, about unusual beliefs... it's really hard to talk about, because I know how it sounds, especially working in healthcare, but... it's just so real to me. 

See, at the hospital, we have to chart everything. Every single thing. Every time I take a set of vitals, every time I empty a Foley catheter, every time I help turn a patient every two hours so they don't get bedsores, I have to log into one of those computers on wheels—we call them COWs—and put it all into the system. But lately, I get this overwhelming feeling, this absolute certainty, that people are tracking my charting. Like they are watching every single keystroke I make, analyzing the timestamps, just waiting and watching me through the system. I don't even know exactly who is doing it, if it's administration or someone else entirely, but I can feel them tracking me. 

And then there are the voices. It's like this whispering, or sometimes it's louder, just right there in my ear when I'm standing in the hallway or even when I'm right in the middle of a patient's room. They say things about me, commenting on what I'm doing, telling me I'm messing up. 

And you'd think—at least, I would think—that with how completely drained I am from that heavy, awful depression I was just telling you about, maybe my brain would just be too tired to do all the other stuff. But it's not. That's the worst part of it all. When the depression is at its absolute worst, when I feel like I'm moving through wet cement and I'm just wishing I could disappear... the voices and the feeling that people are tracking my charting are still right there with it. 

So I’m fighting both at the same time during shifts. I'm dragging this hollow, exhausted body down the fluorescent hallways, trying not to just collapse, and at the exact same time, I'm hearing these voices, and I'm absolutely terrified to type a patient's blood pressure into the computer because I know I'm being monitored. It's just exhausting. I mean, the physical work is hard enough, lifting people and being on your feet for twelve hours, but the mental gymnastics of trying to act completely normal while you're fighting this two-front war in your own head... it just takes everything out of you. Sometimes I'll just go into the clean supply closet and stand there staring at the stacks of extra blankets, just trying to catch my breath, because fighting the heavy feeling and the voices and the tracking all at once... it's just too much.

inference.note: Patient now endorses psychotic symptoms (auditory command/commentary voices and paranoid delusions of being monitored) occurring throughout a prolonged (16-month) depressive episode with passive suicidal ideation. This rules out non-psychotic F32.2/F32.9 and raises F32.3 (severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms) versus F25.1 (schizoaffective disorder, depressive type) if psychotic symptoms persist independent of mood severity.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (voices, feeling monitored) occur only during periods of depressed mood or also occur when the patient's mood is not depressed, to distinguish mood-congruent psychotic depression from schizoaffective disorder
doctor.question: Have there been times when you were not feeling that heavy, depressed mood at all, but you still heard the voices or felt that people were tracking your charting?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a period when my mood had eased up enough that I was running a little again and getting through the day, but for several weeks I still heard comments in empty hallways and kept reading the schedule like it had hidden warnings about me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if there were periods where the psychotic symptoms (voices, delusions about tracking) occurred without the depressed mood, which maps to the Criterion B requirement for schizoaffective disorder.

patient.answer:
Yeah... yeah, actually, there was a time like that. It’s funny you ask, because I remember thinking it was so strange. There was this period when that heavy, wet cement feeling I was telling you about actually eased up. It lifted enough that I felt almost like my old self. I even started running a little again. I used to jog around my neighborhood, just a couple of miles to clear my head, and I had completely stopped doing that when the hollow feeling set in. But for a little bit there, I was actually lacing up my sneakers, getting outside, and just getting through the day without feeling like I was dragging a thousand pounds behind me. I’d wake up and the alarm wouldn’t feel like a punishment. 

But the weird thing is, the other stuff didn't stop. You'd think if my mood was better, my head would clear out entirely, right? But it didn't. For several weeks, even while I was feeling physically okay and getting through my shifts just fine, I was still dealing with it. I’d be walking down to the basement level to grab a bariatric wheelchair or something—totally empty hallway, nobody around at all, just me and the hum of the fluorescent lights—and I’d still hear those comments. Just whispering right there, criticizing me. 

And it wasn't just the voices, either. We have this big printed schedule they pin up on the corkboard in the breakroom, right by the time clock. Even when I was feeling good and running and eating normally, I kept reading that schedule over and over like it had hidden warnings about me. I'd look at the grid and think, okay, why did they shift my lunch break by fifteen minutes? Why am I suddenly floating to the fourth floor on Thursday? I was absolutely convinced whoever was making the schedule was using it to send me coded messages, warning me that they were watching me or that I was in trouble. I’d stand there with my coffee, feeling totally fine energy-wise, but just obsessing over the highlighters and the shift assignments, trying to decode it. So, yeah, even when the depression took a break, that other stuff... it was still right there with me for weeks.

inference.note: Patient confirms psychotic symptoms (voices, delusions of being tracked) persisted for weeks during a period when mood was euthymic and functioning well, ruling out F32.3 (MDD with psychotic features requires psychosis only during mood episodes) and supporting schizoaffective disorder (F25.1). F20.9 added as differential given prominent psychotic symptoms; further clarification on total duration of psychosis relative to mood episodes needed to distinguish between schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia with mood symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine how much of the total 16-month illness duration was spent without an active mood episode (to assess whether psychotic symptoms occurred for a substantial portion of time independent of depression, favoring schizophrenia over schizoaffective disorder)
doctor.question: That period when your mood improved and you were running again but still hearing the voices and feeling tracked—about how many weeks did that stretch last?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a period when my mood had eased up enough that I was running a little again and getting through the day, but for several weeks I still heard comments in empty hallways and kept reading the schedule like it had hidden warnings about me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the period when psychotic symptoms were present without the depressed mood, which directly corresponds to the criterion of experiencing delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think about that... how many weeks exactly. It’s hard to say precisely, because when you work in healthcare, time just sort of blurs together, you know? You’ve got your three twelves, or sometimes you pick up an extra shift because they’re short-staffed and they offer double time, and suddenly a week is gone and you don’t even know what day it is. But... if I really sit down and think about it, looking back at that specific time when I was lacing up my sneakers again and getting out there... 

I’d say it was a solid three, maybe four weeks. Yeah, about a month, give or take a few days. I remember because I had just bought a new pair of running shoes—these bright blue Asics, they have great arch support, which you really need when you're on your feet as much as I am—and I was breaking them in. And during that whole time, that whole three or four-week stretch, my mood was actually okay. Like I said, the heavy, dragging feeling was gone. I wasn't dreading the alarm clock. I was getting up, going for my run, making my coffee, and going into work feeling physically fine. 

But, like I was telling you, the other stuff just wouldn't quit. For that entire month, I’d be walking down to the basement level, completely alone in those empty hallways with just the hum of the fluorescent lights, and I’d still hear those voices making comments about me. Just whispering away. And the breakroom schedule... oh man, I spent that whole three or four weeks just staring at that corkboard. Every single day I clocked in, I’d stand there with my coffee, feeling totally fine energy-wise, but just obsessing over the highlighters and the shift assignments, absolutely convinced it was full of hidden warnings about me. So, yeah, I'd say it was a good three to four weeks where my mood had eased up, but I was still dealing with the voices and the schedule stuff every single day.

inference.note: The patient confirmed a distinct ~3-4 week period of euthymic/improved mood (resumed running, no dragging fatigue) during which the auditory hallucinations and delusions of being tracked/coded messages persisted daily. This satisfies the schizoaffective criterion of psychotic symptoms occurring for a significant period (≥2 weeks) in the absence of mood symptoms, while the depressive episode has still been present for the vast majority (16 of ~16 months) of the illness course. This pattern is inconsistent with F20.9 (schizophrenia), which requires mood episodes to be brief relative to the total duration of psychotic illness, so schizophrenia is ruled out. The findings are most consistent with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type.
